title: Did Last Year's Teachers Fail? Or, a Reflection on the Recursivity of Growing Greater Skills -on-the-recursivity-of-growing-greater-skills
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart builds an argument against blaming prior teachers for a current student's skill gaps, grounding it in a research-cited passage from the Common Core's Appendix A about how grammar and usage development is recursive rather than linear. The Appendix A finding is that learners regress on previously-mastered structures precisely because they're synthesizing new, more complex knowledge, meaning visible errors can be a sign of growth rather than of failed prior instruction. He names his own occupational hazard directly: secondary teachers tend to assume a student's gaps mean someone upstream failed, and he argues this Appendix A paragraph corrects that reflex by reframing errors as evidence that learning boundaries are actively expanding. He generalizes the principle, recursivity, across every subject area, arguing every teacher, regardless of grade level or discipline, must reteach foundational skills at the new grade level's complexity rather than assuming students should already have them locked in. The piece closes by normalizing the messiness of that process: regression during synthesis is what learning looks like, not evidence of a broken system.
points: Stuart cites Common Core Appendix A's research finding that grammar and usage errors reappear as learners synthesize new, more complex structures, reframing regression as a sign of active learning rather than forgotten prior instruction.
He names and pushes back on a specific professional bias: secondary teachers' tendency to blame a student's current gaps on the failure of previous teachers.

His subject-by-subject list (ELA, history, science, Phys Ed) operationalizes recursivity into a concrete expectation: every teacher, at every grade level, must reteach the foundational skills their discipline depends on rather than assuming they should already be there.
quotes: Grammar and usage development in children and in adults rarely follows a linear path. Native speakers and language learners often begin making new errors and seem to lose their mastery of particular grammatical structures or print conventions as they learn new, more complex grammatical structures or new usages of English.

We can tend to assume that if a student doesn't demonstrate competency in something it's because the teachers before him or her failed. It's an ugly tendency, blaming my work problems on the imagined failure of others.

Student errors in my grade level may not be signs of missed learning previously. Instead, they may be signs that new learning is happening and boundaries of capacity are expanding. In other words: errors are promising signs that I'm doing my job.
The best response to errors, then, is teaching. Students will often need to return to the same old topics except at the new grade level's complexity.
That is why, no matter what grade level you teach, you've got to take the time to teach the skills that success requires.

What you just can't do, in other words, is assume that because you teach a certain grade level, the skills should be there. Because even for the hard-working students who've had the hardest-working teachers, the journey isn't finished.
Synthesizing your grade level's complexity is going to look like bouts and fits of regression. That's learning. Messy? Yes. But understandable, too.
